question: to the Commission Kai Tegethoff (Verts/ALE) Subject:

Communities in several Member States have documented a recurring pattern at major infrastructure sites. After a project is permitted and built on the basis of an Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA), the operator makes material operational changes that are not assessed; no new EIA is conducted for those changes; and a parallel sectoral regulatory process (noise review, permit renewal, air-quality plan) is used to adopt the post-change situation as the new environmental baseline, rendering the original assessment unmeasurable. The effect is that Directive 2011/92/EU becomes, in practice, optional for material postconstruction changes. The pattern has been documented at Dublin Airport (complaint CPLT(2026)00881), Amsterdam Schiphol Airport, the ILVA steel plant in Taranto, Groningen Airport Eelde and Berlin Brandenburg Airport. 1.

What is the Commission’s assessment of this recurring pattern, whereby material postconstruction operational changes circumvent the EIA Directive, while a parallel sectoral process redefines the environmental baseline?

Does the Commission consider that Directive 2011/92/EU, as currently drafted and transposed, imposes sufficient requirements as regards the fresh assessment of material post-construction changes that were not assessed in the original consent procedure?

What measures, whether in the form of guidance, infringement action or legislative clarification, is the Commission considering to ensure that material post-construction operational changes are subject to fresh assessment under Directive 2011/92/EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.8.2026) Any changes or extensions to a project listed in Annex I or II of the Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) Directive1 involving works or physical interventions after construction fall within the scope of that Directive and must be subject to an environmental assessment2 or a determination3. The application of the Directive is without prejudice to any requirements under relevant Union environmental legislation. As clarified by the Court of Justice of the EU, the term 'project' under the Directive refers to works and physical interventions4. Changes or extensions to a project after its construction that do not involve any works or interventions altering the physical aspect of a site cannot be classified as a ‘project’ within the meaning of that Directive5. The Commission has issued a notice6 regarding the application of the Directive to changes and extension of projects. The Commission focuses and prioritises its enforcement efforts on the most important and structural breaches of EU law affecting the interests of its citizens and businesses7.
1 Directive 2011/92/EU on the assessment of the effects of certain public and private projects on the

environment, OJ L 26, 28.1.2011, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU, OJ L 124, 25.4.2014. 2 In accordance with Articles 4(1), 5 - 9 of Directive 2011/92/EU. 3 In accordance with Article 4(2) - (6) of Directive 2011/92/EU. 4 Abraham and Others, C-2/07; Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest and Others, C-275/09. 5 Brussels Hoofdstedelijk Gewest and Others, C-275/09; Pro-Braine and Others, C-121/11; Inter-Environnement Wallonie ASBL and Bond Beter Leefmilieu Vlaanderen, C-411/17; Friends of the Irish Environment, C-254/19; Latvijas valsts meži v Dabas aizsardzības pārvalde, C-434/22. 6 Commission notice regarding application of the Environmental Impact Assessment Directive (Directive 2011/92/EU of the European Parliament and of the Council, as amended by Directive 2014/52/EU) to changes and extension of projects - Annex I.24 and Annex II.13(a), including main concepts and principles related to these 2021/C 486/01, OJ C 486, 3.12.2021, pp. 1–19. 7 Communication from the Commission - EU law: Better results through better application, OJ C 18, 19.1.2017, p. 10–20, and Communication from the Commission - Enforcing EU law for a Europe that delivers, 13.10.2022, COM(2022) 518 final.
